answers.text: The caller passes user_id in the query string. The API reads that user's features directly from the online store by user ID, with a 30 ms limit. No cache is used, to keep it simple and fresh.

The store holds one row of the latest feature values per user ID, stamped with its copy time, in the online key-value store. If a run fails or is late, requests keep using the existing rows for up to 6 hours. Older rows count as missing and trigger the popular-items fallback. This comes from the brief.

Fallback triggers: the lookup times out, the user has no features or they are older than 6 hours (all from the brief), and also a model error or timeout, which I added so the user always gets a response. Popular items are recomputed daily and each API instance keeps the latest copy in memory. Where the daily job publishes it is not fixed yet.

Each version stores the model artifact and the features it needs. The registry assigns the number when training registers the model. An alias is a named pointer to one version. Only promote, rollback and shadow-start change aliases, so no redeploy is needed. Who in the team runs those steps is not decided.

Instances poll the registry every 30 seconds and load a new active version in the background. The 30 second poll plus load time keeps rollback under the 1 minute limit. The feature check confirms every feature the model needs exists in the online store. If it fails, the instance keeps its current model and alerts. The 30 second interval is my choice to meet the limit.

Users are chosen by hash(user_id) mod 100 below 10, so a user is always in or out. After responding, the API queues the user ID, features and the active result. The user's response does not depend on the shadow model; a failed enqueue is dropped.

Each worker runs the shadow version on the message and writes one prediction-log row (user, version, items, latency, error flag). Where the log is stored is not decided. If the queue backs up, new messages are dropped. A worker failure is logged and not retried, since shadow data is only a sample.

It reads the prediction log and outputs a report for the ML lead with days in shadow, error rate, p99 inference latency and item overlap with active. The criteria are from the brief: at least 7 days in shadow, error under 0.5%, p99 inference under 80 ms, and ML lead approval. I added the overlap metric as a decision.

answers.text: The response has the same shape either way: items (20 IDs) plus a boolean fallback flag. A fallback returns the 20 popular IDs with fallback true. A flag is the simplest way for callers to tell them apart.

The model call gets 80 ms, matching the 80 ms p99 inference limit for promotion. 30 ms lookup plus 80 ms leaves about 40 ms for the rest of the 150 ms budget. If the model call passes 80 ms it counts as an error and the popular fallback is returned. The 80 ms figure is my choice.

The check compares the feature names the model needs with the online store's feature list, not any user's row. It runs only at model load time (API instances and shadow workers). A single user with missing features is handled per request by the no-fresh-features fallback.

At startup an instance loads the active version before it is marked ready, so it takes no traffic without a model. If the first load fails it stays not ready and alerts. I chose this over serving only popular items because it avoids silently serving degraded responses.

Yes, workers poll the registry every 30 seconds and load in the background like API instances. On an alias change they keep the old version until the new one loads, and each row records the version used. If the shadow alias is unset or nothing is loaded, they drop messages and write no rows.

Shadow-start is a manual command that sets the shadow alias to a registered version. Nothing triggers it automatically after registration. Who runs it is not decided and is listed as an open question.

The promote command, run by the ML lead for one candidate version, checks that version's report against the criteria and refuses if they are not met. Running it is the approval and it records who and when. It then performs the switch. Days in shadow count only for the version in question, and only days it held the shadow alias. Whether days must be consecutive is not decided.

answers.text: The loaded model is held in memory in each instance. The background load finishes first, then the instance swaps its reference in one step. Requests already running finish on the old model, so none are dropped. Added one clause to step 4.

Each materialization run writes the list of feature names it copies, and the feature check reads that list. So the list changes when the job's copied features change, and no one updates it by hand. Added to step 1.

I decided the model runs in-process in the API instance (loaded from the registry), with the user's feature row as input; stated in step 3. I do not know what candidate pool the 20 items are ranked from or how the instance gets it. Added to Open questions rather than guessing.

An instance loads the popular list at startup and is not ready until it has it (step 4). If the daily recompute fails, instances keep the last copy (step 3). The fallback reads memory only, so it cannot fail at request time. Where the daily job publishes the list is listed as undecided.

If the previous version fails load or the feature check on an instance, that instance keeps the model it has (the one active before the rollback) and raises an alert, so the person on call is told. I chose this over taking the instance out of service because serving the old model is better than serving nothing. Step 4 now says this covers a rollback target.

The question found a real gap. The log row had no active items and no time. The queue message already carried the active items, so I made each row also store the time, the active version and its items. The job takes overlap from those columns and days in shadow from the dates of the rows. Changed steps 5 and 6.

Promote checks the latest report for that version. It refuses if there is no report from the last 24 hours, and it also refuses if the candidate is no longer the shadow alias. This keeps a stale or switched-away report from being used for approval. The 24 hour limit is my choice, matching the daily job. Changed step 7.

teachbacks.text:
1. Background job, hourly (materialization). A job copies features from the warehouse into the online store, one row per user, and stamps each row with its copy time. Each run also writes the feature list, which is the names of the features it copied. If a run fails, requests keep using the rows already there. Rows older than 6 hours count as missing.

2. Model registration, when training finishes. Training registers a model in the model registry. The registry assigns the next version number, and the version is immutable. It stores the list of features that version needs. Nothing starts shadow automatically after training. Only three actions change aliases: shadow-start, promote and rollback. Aliases are named pointers: `active`, `previous` and `shadow`.

3. Instance startup. An API instance loads the active version and the popular list before it is marked ready. If that first load fails, the instance stays not ready and raises an alert. The popular list is recomputed daily, and each instance keeps the latest copy in memory. If a recompute fails, instances keep the last copy.

4. Ongoing model loading, every 30 seconds. Each instance checks the registry. If the active alias points to a new version, the instance loads it in the background. It then runs the feature check, which compares the names of the features the model needs against the feature list. It never looks at a user's row. If the check passes, the instance swaps to the new model in one step, and requests already running finish on the old model. If the check or the load fails, including when the target is a rollback target, the instance keeps its current model and alerts. This is how a promotion or rollback reaches instances without a redeploy, within 1 minute.

5. The request arrives. The home page calls `GET /recommendations?user_id=...`. The API instance handles it. The total p99 budget is 150 ms.

6. Feature lookup. The API reads that user's feature row from the online store, which holds the latest features keyed by user ID. The limit is 30 ms and there is no cache. If the lookup times out, or the row is missing or older than 6 hours, the API skips to step 8 and returns the fallback.

7. Model call. The API runs the active model, held in memory in that instance, on the row. The limit is 80 ms. It returns 20 item IDs. If the model errors or passes 80 ms, the API returns the fallback.

8. Response. A normal response is `{"items": [...20 IDs], "fallback": false}`. The fallback has the same shape, with 20 popular IDs read from the in-memory popular list and `"fallback": true`. The fallback reads only memory, so the document says it cannot fail at request time.

9. Shadow copy, after the response is sent. A user is in shadow if hash(user_id) mod 100 is below 10, so a given user is always in or always out of shadow. For those users the API puts a message on the shadow queue. The message holds the user ID, the features, the active version's number and the active items. Sending is fire-and-forget. If it fails or the queue is full, the message is dropped. The user's response never waits on or uses shadow output.

10. Shadow worker. Workers read from the shadow queue. They load the shadow-alias version the same way instances do. They check every 30 seconds, load a changed version in the background, and run the feature check. If the check fails, that version does not run. A worker keeps its current version until a new one has loaded. For each message it runs its loaded shadow version and writes one prediction-log row. The row holds the time, user, shadow version, shadow items, active version, active items, latency, and whether it errored. Each row records the version actually used. If the shadow alias is unset or no version is loaded, the worker drops the message and writes no row. A worker error is logged and not retried.

11. How a candidate gets into shadow. A person runs the manual shadow-start command, which sets the shadow alias to a registered version. Step 10 then picks it up.

12. Daily comparison, once a day. A job reads the prediction log and writes a dated report for the ML lead, per shadow version. The report has days in shadow (distinct dates of that version's rows, counting only days it held the shadow alias), error rate, p99 inference latency, and overlap between the version's items and the active items stored in the same row.

13. Promote. The ML lead reads the report and runs the promote command for one candidate version. The command refuses unless all of these hold. The version is the current shadow alias. It has a report from the last 24 hours. That report shows at least 7 days in shadow, error rate under 0.5% and p99 inference latency under 80 ms. Running the command counts as the ML lead's approval, and it records who ran it and when. On success it moves the active alias to the candidate, and the old active version becomes `previous`. The instances then pick up the change through step 4. Whether a live A/B test comes between shadow and this switch is undecided, and the plan says it works either way.

14. Rollback. A person moves the active alias back to `previous`. Instances pick it up within 1 minute through step 4. If the load or feature check fails for the rollback target, instances keep their current model and alert.

Failure summary. Most request-path failures return the fallback. Materialization failures leave old rows in use until they pass 6 hours. A first-load failure leaves the instance not ready. Later load or check failures keep the current model and alert. Shadow failures never touch the response. A promote whose criteria are not met, or whose report is stale, is refused.
gaps: What candidate pool the model ranks the 20 items from, and how the API gets it, is not stated. This stops me explaining how step 7 turns a feature row into 20 item IDs. The document lists it as an open question.
How the fallback chooses which 20 items to return from the popular list is not stated. It does not say whether the list is global or personalised, or how its 20 are picked.
Who is allowed to run shadow-start, promote and rollback is undecided. The document lists it as an open question.

How the active and shadow aliases are changed is only partly described. Shadow-start, promote and rollback are named as commands or actions, but the document does not say what the rollback action looks like.
